newsitem.title: GERMANY: German unions step up threats in sick pay dispute.
newsitem.headline: German unions step up threats in sick pay dispute.

text.p: German trade unions said on Sunday they would make no concessions in a sick pay dispute threatening to throw German industrial relations into turmoil ahead of wider 1997 wage talks.

At issue is a federal law passed in September aimed at allowing employers to cut sick pay allowances from the current 100 percent of salary to 80 percent, a move which would shave some 12 billion marks off German industry's labour costs.
Germany has some of the most generous sick pay and holiday provisions in the world.

Industrial giant Daimler-Benz AG, the first large company seeking to implement the law, was last week forced to delay the cuts after more 100,000 of its workers walked out, protesting that it breached existing wage contracts.

"When employers force us into conflict, we shall not simply step down," Ursula Engelen-Kefer, deputy head of the DGB federation of German trade unions, said in an interview with the Bild am Sonntag newspaper on Sunday.

DAG, the white-collar workers union that has threatened banks with industrial action if they implement the cuts, renewed calls for trade unions to fight together against the sick pay cuts and other planned benefit reductions.

"The 'Programme for Growth and Jobs' is a complete misuse of language," DAG chairman Roland Issen told German radio, referring to Chancellor Helmut Kohl's austerity package which provided for the cost-cutting measures.

While banks and other firms such as chemical giant BASF AG have now, despite worker protests, also revealed their intention to introduce the cuts, confrontation is still most likely to flare in the engineering sector first.
With an uneasy truce on industrial action now in place between metalworkers and employers, ultimatums have been issued on both sides before scheduled talks can restart on October 21.

Werner Stumpfe, chairman of the Gesamtmetall employers group, has stated as an "absolute pre-condition" for future negotiations that the issue of sick pay and other benefits be included in wider 1997 wage talks.
IG Metall for its part is demanding that Gesamtmetall make clear its final position on sick pay by October 23 -- a day before a second day of countrywide protests in the sector has been planned.

Engelen-Kefer on Sunday repeated the offer of a compromise under which sick payments calculated on basic salary alone -- rather than the current system where overtime wages are taken into account -- could be discussed.
But union leaders know that such an offer is likely to find little favour with Gesamtmetall.

With German business clammering for reductions in labour costs, it will be trying to secure a deal that includes not only sick pay cuts but also reductions on existing benefits such as holiday pay and generous Christmas bonuses.

Unless real reductions in overall employment costs are available, Gesamtmetall has said it could not agree even to the 1997 real wage freeze IG Metall has said it would settle for in exchange for job protection guarantees.
Gesamtmetall's Stumpfe said earlier this week that now not only the 1997 wage deal was at stake but the whole future of Germany's system of collective wage bargaining.
